stops.title: The question
stops.text: So far every paper made each network call cheaper by storing weights in fewer bits. DeepCache attacks a different cost: the number of times the deep part of the network runs at all. Its question is simple. If a diffusion model does fifty denoising steps, does it really need to recompute everything fifty times? The answer is no, and the fix needs no training and no calibration data. That matters here, because step caching is the other lever the thesis can pull on LTX-2.3.

stops.title: The big picture
stops.text: Here is the whole idea in one drawing. On the left, the normal sampler runs the full U-Net at every step. On the right, DeepCache with an interval N of three. The first step runs the full network and stores its deep feature, shown in indigo. The next two steps run only the shallow top blocks and plug that stored feature back in. So the expensive deep part runs once and is reused twice. Everything else in the paper refines where to cache and how often.

stops.title: Why the waste exists
stops.text: Why is this allowed? Sampling is a long chain of calls to the same network, each costing about the same. Existing fixes either take fewer steps, or prune and distill the model, which means retraining on millions of images. The authors noticed something simpler. The deep, high-level features barely move between neighbouring steps, with cosine similarity often above 0.95. So most of the deep compute at each step repeats work already done. That redundancy is the gap DeepCache exploits.

stops.title: Where the cache lives
stops.text: Now the mechanism. A U-Net pairs each down block with an up block through a skip connection. The main branch in the middle is deep and expensive. DeepCache stores the feature that flows up the main branch into a shallow up block. On a reuse step, only the first down block and the matching up block run, and fresh detail from the new input still arrives through the skip. For Stable Diffusion the paper keeps branch two, which costs only about eleven percent of the full compute.

stops.title: When to refresh
stops.text: The second knob is which steps run the full network. The simple version refreshes every N steps. But features change faster in some parts of the process than others. So the non-uniform schedule packs full steps around a centre point where similarity between steps is lowest, and spaces them out further away from it. Both rows here spend the same budget of ten full steps out of fifty. Notice this is only a list of step indices, pure sampling loop logic.

stops.title: The catch for LTX-2.3
stops.text: Before the results, the part that concerns this project directly. LTX-2 is not a U-Net. It is a flat stack of equal-cost transformer blocks joined by residual adds, with no long skip to carry fresh detail around a cached middle. So the recipe cannot be copied literally. What transfers is the principle that features change slowly across timesteps. For a transformer, the thing to cache is the change a span of middle blocks adds, or the whole model output, as TeaCache does. This drawing is the tab's own illustration.

stops.title: Does it work?
stops.text: This chart is the comparison that matters. It plots text alignment, the CLIP score, against speed-up for Stable Diffusion. The fair rival is simply taking fewer sampling steps, and that line falls steadily. DeepCache keeps fifty steps and raises the interval, and the non-uniform version stays almost flat up to about 2.3 times. At N of five it reaches 2.15 times faster with a CLIP score of 29.46, against 29.51 for the original. The cost appears at large intervals, where fine details start to drift.

stops.title: What the thesis takes from it
stops.text: So what goes into the thesis? Caching changes the sampling loop, not the weights, so it stacks on top of NNCF int8 or int4 compression. But quantization noise and stale features add up, so the combination should be measured, not each part alone. On OpenVINO, the transformer is exported as two or three sub-models and the Python loop decides each step. Little gain is expected on a few-step distilled model, and the comparison should always include fewer steps. Next, TeaCache replaces the fixed interval with an adaptive trigger built for exactly these transformers.
